description: Madonna's breakthrough dance-pop single from her 1983 debut album, written by Pure Energy's Curtis Hudson and Lisa Stevens-Crowder. A last-minute addition that became her first Billboard chart-topper on the dance chart.

pops.text: It started as a ballad! Lisa Stevens-Crowder came up with the chord progression, and Curtis Hudson turned it into an uptempo celebration.
Hudson said he wrote the lyrics in about 30 minutes, watching grim news on TV and wishing the whole world could take one day off.
Pure Energy's own label, Prism Records, passed on the demo. So did singer Phyllis Hyman and Mary Wilson of the Supremes.
Producer John 'Jellybean' Benitez brought it to Madonna when her debut album still needed one more song. It was his first production from scratch.
No pressure: Warner Bros. gave Benitez one week to finish the track at New York's Sigma Sound Studios, or it would miss the album.
That cowbell at the start? Madonna played it herself. Songwriter Curtis Hudson played guitar, and his brother Raymond played bass.
Fred Zarr added the piano solo near the end — Madonna called those flourishes his 'Zarrisms.'
Clubs got it first: Benitez debuted it at the Fun House, and DJ Larry Levan spun it at the Paradise Garage before it was even a single.
Released September 7, 1983, it became Madonna's first No. 1 on a Billboard chart, topping Dance Club Songs, and reached No. 16 on the Hot 100.

On American Bandstand in January 1984, Dick Clark asked about her dreams. Madonna's answer: 'To rule the world.' In the UK the song hit the Top 10 three separate times — in 1985 it sat at No. 2, kept off the top by her own 'Into the Groove.'

title: Holiday

description: Madonna's definitive dance-floor anthem, written with Stephen Bray for the 1985 film Desperately Seeking Susan. Never a US commercial single, it still became her first UK No. 1 and her biggest seller there.

pops.text: This was not written for Madonna! She and Stephen Bray wrote it for Cheyne, a teenage protege of DJ and producer Mark Kamins, who financed the demo.
Madonna wrote it in her fourth-floor Avenue B walk-up, watching a handsome Puerto Rican man across the street she hoped to date. She later called the song 'dorky.'
Her real inspiration, she said, was the dance floor itself — a magical, freeing place for a trained dancer turned singer.
Stuck on the bridge in the studio, Madonna improvised the line 'Live out your fantasy here with me' — and it solved the song on the spot.
Director Susan Seidelman needed music for a nightclub scene in Desperately Seeking Susan, so Madonna offered this demo. Kamins was furious she had kept it for herself.
Contract tangles kept it off the film's soundtrack album, even though the song and the movie are now inseparable.
The video is simply clips from Desperately Seeking Susan — no separate video shoot was ever made for one of her biggest hits.
In the US it was never a commercial single, only the B-side of the 12-inch 'Angel,' so it was ineligible for the Billboard Hot 100.
That 'Angel / Into the Groove' pairing still topped Billboard's dance sales chart, and Billboard later named it the Dance Single of the Decade for the 1980s.
In Britain it was a standalone single: her first UK No. 1, four weeks at the top, and it remains her biggest-selling single there. It was later added to the 1985 reissue of Like a Virgin.

title: Into the Groove

description: A soaring, faith-questioning highlight of My Morning Jacket's 2005 album Z, built on Andrew Bird's looped strings and Jim James's attempt, in his words, to scream away the horrors of the world.

pops.text: Track three on Z, released October 4, 2005 — the album that remade My Morning Jacket's sound in just 10 tighter, spacier songs.
Z was the band's first album with an outside producer. Jim James had produced everything himself before hiring John Leckie, of Stone Roses and Radiohead's The Bends fame.
It was also their first record made away from Kentucky, recorded at Allaire Studios in New York's Catskill Mountains instead of the family farm.
New guys, new sound: guitarist Carl Broemel and keyboardist Bo Koster had just replaced two founding members, and were the first two players to audition.
Leckie largely dialed back the band's signature cavernous reverb, pushing James's voice up front instead of burying it in a grain silo.
That strange string swirl at the start is Andrew Bird, layering strings through a looper pedal and an octave pedal. Bird also whistles and plays strings elsewhere on Z.
The band could not take Bird on tour, so they sampled that opening. To this day, Bo Koster triggers Bird's strings live before the band crashes in over them.
James said the song was him trying to scream away the horrors of the world, like an abstract painting — angry about the state of things, but deliberately timeless, not tied to one headline.
Its heart is a plea about faith: religion should appeal to the hearts of the young, believe what you want, James says — just do not force it on anyone else.

Gideon was released as a single in 2006, and the band played it on David Letterman's show that year with the Boston Pops Orchestra. Z later landed on Rolling Stone's 500 Greatest Albums of All Time list.

title: Gideon

description: The gentle road song at the heart of My Morning Jacket's 2003 major-label breakthrough It Still Moves — part love letter, part tour diary, ending on heaven's golden shore.

pops.text: Track three on It Still Moves, released in 2003 — the Louisville band's third album and the one that carried their reverb-drenched Americana to a much bigger audience.
It opens mid-tour: 'Watchin' a stretch of road, miles of light explode' — James watching highways and crowds roll in, night after night.
James explained the first half is a young musician's wide-eyed wonder at life on the road, experiencing everything for the first time.
The second half turns homeward, he said: balancing love against the adventure, fortunate to have someone promise, 'If you'll be here for me, I'll be here for you.'
In a later podcast deep-dive on this song, James also traced it to a struggling relationship — and a warning from his grandmother.
The chorus shrugs at barroom wisdom — 'people always told me that bars are dark and lonely' — then chooses one person over all of it.
Hear a little frog in that tender high vocal? James counts Kermit the Frog and the Muppets among his formative influences, and he means it sincerely.
The Kermit connection came full circle in 2019, when James sang 'Rainbow Connection' alongside Kermit himself at the Newport Folk Festival.
Golden was in the set for the band's legendary rain-soaked Bonnaroo performance in June 2004. That set was released in 2023 as MMJ Live Vol. 3: Bonnaroo 2004 (Return to Thunderdome).
When It Still Moves was remixed and remastered for a deluxe reissue in 2016, it came with James's original demos — including an early, stripped-back demo of Golden, premiered by NPR.

title: Golden

description: The second single from the international edition of Of Monsters and Men's debut My Head Is an Animal (2011), a run-through-the-woods folk-pop anthem from Iceland that topped US adult alternative radio.

pops.text: Run! The whole song is an escape into the wild — through the woods, deep into the mountain sound, sleeping under stars to outrun trouble back home.
It was written by the band's two singers, Nanna Bryndis Hilmarsdottir and Ragnar Thorhallsson, with drummer Arnar Rosenkranz Hilmarsson, and produced by Jacquire King.
Nanna and Ragnar share the lead vocal, trading and joining voices — the boy-girl call-and-response that became the band's signature.
A music nerd's detail: the song is in 2/2 time and E major, which helps give that galloping, half-time stomp its forward push.
It did not appear on the original Icelandic album in that form — it arrived as a single from the international version of My Head Is an Animal, released September 2, 2012.
This video is a real gig, not a staged shoot: the band performing at a festival in Reykjavik's Hljomskalagardurinn park on July 7, 2012. It premiered that September.
Rolling Stone called the song 'upbeat, barreling,' and The Guardian singled out its chorus built around the very English-sounding line 'Hold your horses now.'
American radio loved it: it reached No. 1 on Billboard's Adult Alternative chart in 2012-13 and spent a full 52 weeks on Billboard's Hot Rock Songs chart.
It went Platinum in the United States, certified by the RIAA in January 2015, and Platinum in Australia too.
Afterlife: you can hear it in the trailer for the film Alexander and the Terrible, Horrible, No Good, Very Bad Day, and play it in Guitar Hero Live and as downloadable content for Rock Band 4.

title: Mountain Sound

description: A slow-burning ballad from the Icelandic sextet's debut album My Head Is an Animal, with Nanna Bryndís Hilmarsdóttir out front — the quiet, steady heart of a record built on monsters, myths and big choruses.

pops.text: Track four on the band's debut album, My Head Is an Animal — and true to its title, it's the record's slow burn, building gently for a full five minutes.
Home first: the album was released in Iceland on 20 September 2011. The rest of the world had to wait until April 2012, when Republic Records put it out internationally.
The album's title isn't random poetry — 'My head is an animal' is the second line of the opening track, 'Dirty Paws.'
Before any of this, the band won Músíktilraunir, Iceland's annual battle-of-the-bands competition, in 2010 — the launchpad for a string of Icelandic acts before them.
This was never meant to be a band at all: Of Monsters and Men began as Nanna's solo project, then grew, friend by friend, into a six-piece.
Most of the album trades lines between Nanna and Ragnar Þórhallsson, but here Nanna takes the lead — reviewers singled out her shining vocal on this lavish ballad.
This track was produced by Jacquire King, the Nashville producer behind Kings of Leon's 'Use Somebody.' He worked on four of the album's songs.
The video you're watching was made by WeWereMonkeys, a Canadian production firm that created the album's whole video series, drawing on Nordic mythology and the lyrics.
The parent album debuted at No. 6 on the Billboard 200 with 55,000 copies sold — at the time, a US chart record for an Icelandic artist.
Not a single, never a hit — just a fan-favorite deep cut. Sometimes the tortoise really does win the race: slow and steady.

title: Slow And Steady

description: Paul McCartney and Wings' glam-rock blast from Band on the Run — the album's first single, a Top 10 hit on both sides of the Atlantic, and named for a McCartney family pet. Jet! Jet!

pops.text: First things first: 'Jet' was the first single released from Band on the Run, ahead of the title track.
Who is Jet? Paul has told it two ways — for years, a black Labrador puppy from a litter at home; in his 2021 book The Lyrics, a little Shetland pony belonging to his daughter Mary.
Paul wrote it at his farm in Scotland: 'I was in a songwriting mood and I was up in Scotland. I just thought, OK, I just gotta go somewhere and try and write a song.'
Plot twist: unlike most of Band on the Run, 'Jet' was NOT recorded in Lagos, Nigeria. It was cut back in London at George Martin's AIR Studios.
Take two: Wings first tried recording it on 3 October 1973 and scrapped the attempt. The remake from 9 October became the album version.
That's Paul on drums on the backing track — with Wings down to a trio, he also added bass and piano, while Linda played the synthesizer part.
Hear that saxophone wailing through it? That's Howie Casey, brought in for the London sessions after Wings got home from Lagos.
Engineer Geoff Emerick noticed oxide building up on the tape heads and secretly copied 'Jet' onto a fresh reel — he never told Paul, and credits that rescue with the song's solid sound.
Chart flight: 'Jet' peaked at No. 7 in both the US and the UK in March 1974 — and flew even higher in New Zealand, reaching No. 2.
Name stealers: Australian rock band Jet took their name directly from this song — McCartney and The Beatles were a huge influence on them.

title: Jet

description: Wings' three-part escape epic — prison lament, breakout and joyride in a single song. It's the title track of their Lagos-recorded 1973 classic, and it topped the US chart in 1974.

pops.text: One song, three songs: 'Band on the Run' is a medley of three distinct musical passages, and at 5:09 it's one of McCartney's longest-ever singles.
'If I ever get out of here' came from George Harrison, who said something like it during one of The Beatles' endless Apple business meetings — Paul remembered it years later.
Days before the Lagos trip, drummer Denny Seiwell and guitarist Henry McCullough quit Wings. No time for replacements: the 'band' that flew to Nigeria was Paul, Linda and Denny Laine.
Paul picked Lagos for an exotic recording adventure. He found an EMI studio that was below standard, in a city where conditions were tense and difficult.
The low point: Paul and Linda were robbed at knifepoint on a walk, losing a bag containing unfinished song lyrics and the album's demo tapes. The songs had to be rebuilt from memory.
And the punchline arrived later: back in London, the McCartneys received a letter from EMI — dated before they left — warning them not to go to Lagos because of a cholera outbreak.
The famous album cover was shot at Osterley Park, west London, on 28 October 1973 by Clive Arrowsmith: the three Wings members plus six celebrity 'convicts' caught in a prison searchlight.
Name the escapees: chat-show host Michael Parkinson, singer Kenny Lynch, actors James Coburn and Christopher Lee, politician Clement Freud, and boxer John Conteh.
Parkinson later said Paul promised to appear on his chat show in exchange for the cover shoot. Paul finally kept the promise in 1999 — 26 years later.
The great escape worked: the single hit No. 1 in the US on 8 June 1974, sold over a million copies there, and reached No. 3 in the UK.

title: Band On The Run

description: Paul Simon's horn-fired 1980 hit from One-Trick Pony, built on Steve Gadd's Mozambique drum groove. The film flopped; this song danced to No. 6 and never really left the stage.

pops.text: Lead single from One-Trick Pony, released in July 1980 — and Paul Simon's first single for Warner Bros. Records after leaving Columbia.
One-Trick Pony was also a film: Simon wrote it and starred as Jonah Levin, a once-popular folk-rocker on the slide. The movie flopped; the song did not.
It was his first new studio album in five years, since Still Crazy After All These Years in 1975 — Simon took his time, then came back dancing.
That irresistible drum groove is drummer Steve Gadd playing a New York City-style Cuban Mozambique pattern — drummers still study it.
Gadd's trick: he played with two pairs of drumsticks, one pair in each hand, creating the illusion of two drummers playing together. He demonstrates it in drum clinics.
The band is a session-player dream team — Tony Levin on bass, Eric Gale on guitar, Richard Tee on piano — and they played Simon's backing band in the film, too.
Billboard praised the song's horn interlude and called the hook built on its 'percussive and bass duet' irresistible. Hard to argue while dancing.
Chart split: No. 6 on the US Billboard Hot 100, Top 20 in the Netherlands, Belgium and New Zealand — but only No. 58 in the UK. Britain, explain yourself.
The song earned Simon a Grammy nomination, and the album's reputation has quietly grown ever since — the flop film's soundtrack that outlived the film.
Afterlife: Simon performed it with Art Garfunkel at their famous 1981 reunion concert in Central Park — it stayed a fixture of his live shows for decades.

title: Late in the Evening

description: Paul Simon's Graceland calling card — a midlife crisis you can dance to, complete with a backwards bass solo and Chevy Chase stealing the video. Call him Al; just don't call him Paul at a party.

pops.text: Lead single from Graceland, released in July 1986 with 'Gumboots' on the B-side — a taste of the South African sounds Simon had fallen for.
Al and Betty are real mix-ups: at a party, French composer Pierre Boulez mistakenly called Paul 'Al' and his wife Peggy 'Betty.' Simon kept the names and built a chorus on them.
Under the bounce, it's a midlife crisis: 'Why am I soft in the middle? The rest of my life is so hard.' Simon was 44 when Graceland came out.
The song started with a riff from South African guitarist Ray Phiri, one of the Johannesburg musicians Simon recorded Graceland with.
That famous bass solo is a palindrome: Bakithi Kumalo played the first half, then engineer Roy Halee reversed the tape for the second half, so it folds back on itself.
The penny whistle solo is by Morris Goldberg, a South African-born jazz musician — that's him Simon mimes along with in the video.
This beloved video was actually take two: Simon disliked the first one, a performance filmed during his Saturday Night Live hosting monologue, so a replacement was cooked up with Lorne Michaels.

Director Gary Weis put Chevy Chase in a pink-walled room lip-syncing ALL of Simon's lead vocals, while Simon deadpans the backing parts and mimes instruments. Chase said he learned the song on the way to the shoot.
The height gag is real: Chase stands about 6'4" to Simon's roughly 5'3" — the video leans into it, down to their synchronized little dance in the bridge.

Slow-burn hit: it first peaked at No. 44 in the US, then re-entered the chart after Graceland won the Album of the Year Grammy and climbed to No. 23 — Simon's last US Top 40 hit. In the UK it reached No. 4.

title: You Can Call Me Al

description: Pet Shop Boys turn Catholic-school guilt into maximal synth-pop theatre on the lead single from Actually. It topped charts across Europe, reached the US top 10, and remains one of only two songs played on every Pet Shop Boys tour.

pops.text: Written in 1982 in a Camden studio: Chris Lowe played chords that sounded to Neil Tennant like a hymn, and the phrase 'it's a sin' arrived on the spot.
Tennant says he wrote it in about 15 minutes as a camp joke. A Newcastle parish priest still delivered a sermon reflecting on it.
The demo was in Tennant's pocket when he first took New York producer Bobby Orlando to lunch. They cut another demo with Orlando in 1984, but it stayed unreleased.
The lyrics revisit Tennant's years at St Cuthbert's Grammar School in Newcastle, where he felt everything pleasurable was taught to be sinful.
Listen to the coda: Tennant recites part of the Confiteor in Latin — 'through my fault, through my fault, through my most grievous fault.'
For ambience, the team recorded at London's Brompton Oratory and Westminster Cathedral. The sung Mass they captured happened to be in the song's key, C minor — its 'amen' closes the track.
Producer Julian Mendelsohn built the record, but the duo had Stephen Hague remix it. Hague's version is the single and album take you know.
Released 15 June 1987, it spent three weeks at UK No. 1, topped charts in more than 15 other countries, and reached No. 9 on the Billboard Hot 100.
DJ Jonathan King publicly claimed the melody was lifted from Cat Stevens' 'Wild World' and even released his own version to prove it. The duo sued, won damages, and donated them to charity.

Derek Jarman's video casts Tennant before an inquisition, Lowe as his jailer and Ron Moody as judge, cut with the seven deadly sins. In 2021, Russell T Davies named his AIDS-crisis drama It's a Sin after the song, sending its streams up nearly 250%.

title: It's a Sin

description: First released in 1984, then re-recorded for debut album Please, this moody London travelogue about class and inner-city pressure became Pet Shop Boys' first No. 1 in both the UK and the US.

pops.text: In 1983 Smash Hits journalist Neil Tennant met producer Bobby Orlando in New York while on assignment to interview Sting. Orlando heard the duo's demos and offered to produce — aiming for a rap record in a British accent.
Orlando played most of the instruments on the first version himself. Its drum part was lifted from Michael Jackson's 'Billie Jean,' over what Tennant called 'Barry White chords.'
The original single came out in April 1984 on Bobcat Records. It became a club hit in Los Angeles and San Francisco, but in Britain it was only available as a 12-inch import.
The opening lines — 'Sometimes you're better off dead, there's a gun in your hand…' — came to Tennant at his cousin's house in Nottingham, falling asleep after watching a gangster film.
The lyrics borrow narrative voices and arcane references from T. S. Eliot's poem The Waste Land. Tennant later clarified the song is 'about rough boys getting a bit of posh.'

The hit re-recording with Stephen Hague took a full week at Advision Studios. Engineer David Jacob said it was built from just four rhythm patterns, with one real cymbal as the only 'real' instrument.

That opening traffic noise? Hague recorded it on Gosfield Street outside the studio with a Sony Professional Walkman. The faint voice at the start turned out to be a passing WHAM! fan saying 'Get on the mic-ro-ph-one.'
The 'trumpet solo' is Hague playing an Emulator sampler. It reportedly took about six hours — deliberately playing wrong notes to make it sound more like real jazz.
Re-released in October 1985, it hit No. 1 in the UK in January 1986 and topped the Billboard Hot 100 that May — among the first rap-influenced songs to top both charts.

Honours kept coming: Best Single at the 1987 Brit Awards, Song of the Decade 1985–1994 from the British Academy of Composers and Songwriters, and No. 1 in The Guardian's 2020 poll of the greatest UK No. 1 singles. The duo performed it at the 2012 London Olympics closing ceremony.

title: West End Girls

description: Phish's beloved Rolling Stones cover, filmed at Festival 8 on Halloween 2009 as part of their full Exile on Main St. 'musical costume' and released in the 2010 concert film Phish 3D, horns and Sharon Jones included.

pops.text: Origin story: 'Loving Cup' is a Rolling Stones song, written by Mick Jagger and Keith Richards and released on Exile on Main St. on 12 May 1972. It's the album's ninth track.

The Stones first recorded an early version between April and July 1969 at Olympic Studios in London during the Let It Bleed sessions, with a completely different piano intro. Part of it surfaced on the 2010 deluxe Exile reissue.

On the Stones' final version, the piano is session great Nicky Hopkins, with Bobby Keys on saxophone and Jim Price on trumpet and trombone. Producer Jimmy Miller even plays the maracas — and guitarist Mick Taylor doesn't play on it at all.
The Stones played it at Hyde Park on 5 July 1969, where Jagger introduced it under a different name: 'Gimme a Little Drink.'

Phish debuted their cover on 3 February 1993 in Portland, Maine. JamBase notes the song arrived to showcase Page McConnell's new baby grand piano — those rolling piano lines have anchored their version ever since.
It's since become one of Phish's most cherished covers. Their versions appear on live albums including At the Roxy, Hampton/Winston-Salem '97 and Amsterdam.
Big-occasion song: Phish closed their first show back from breakup — Hampton Coliseum, 6 March 2009 — with a 'Loving Cup' encore, after an a cappella 'Grind' and 'Bouncing Around the Room.'

This performance is Halloween night, 31 October 2009, at Festival 8 in Indio, California, where Phish played all of Exile on Main St. as their 'musical costume.' Fans learned the choice from a Phishbill handed out at the gates.
Phish didn't play Exile alone: a horn section joined them, and Sharon Jones and Saundra Williams sang backing vocals on 'Loving Cup' — adding gospel weight the Stones' original only hinted at.

Footage became the film Phish 3D, which opened in theatres on 30 April 2010. Weeks later Phish played 'Loving Cup' on Late Night with Jimmy Fallon during Stones Week — introduced by Keith Richards himself.

title: Loving Cup

description: Trey Anastasio's surreal waiter tale from A Picture of Nectar, Phish's 1992 major-label debut. Its chorus — 'Your hands and feet are mangoes, you're gonna be a genius anyway' — hides a surprisingly moving origin.

pops.text: Written entirely by Trey Anastasio, says Phish.net. Phish's own site sums up the verses perfectly: 'a day in the life of a waiter/addict with delusions of grandeur.'
Phish.net traces the chorus to a film idea by Trey's friend Aaron Woolf: a boy in war-torn Vietnam is left with severely mangled hands and feet, yet grows up to excel intellectually.
One line of Woolf's pitch — 'his hands and feet are mangled' — stuck in Anastasio's head. Slightly twisted, it became 'Your hands and feet are mangoes… you're gonna be a genius anyway.'

The surreal verses — spasm waiters, squeeze cheese, grape apple pies — are rumoured, per Phish.net, to draw partly on Anastasio's own restaurant days, where much of the waiting staff indulged heavily.
Phish first played it live on 30 March 1989 at The Front in Burlington, Vermont — nearly three years before it reached an album.
It was recorded in summer 1991 at White Crow Studios in the band's hometown of Burlington, Vermont, mostly before Phish had even signed their Elektra deal.
Home album A Picture of Nectar was released on 18 February 1992. It was Phish's third studio album — and their major-label debut on Elektra Records. 'The Mango Song' sits as track 12, running 6:24.
The album is dedicated to Nectar Rorris, owner of Nectar's in Burlington, where Phish played their first bar gig and a run of monthly three-night stands that taught them how to be a band.

Even the band found this one slippery: in an interview around the album's release, Mike Gordon singled out 'Mango' as perhaps the only song on Nectar that couldn't be pigeonholed into a specific genre.

A Picture of Nectar was certified gold by the RIAA on 15 November 2001. Live, 'Mango' turned into a relative rarity in the mid-'90s — though a few 2000 versions stretched this normally tightly shut song past 15 minutes of improvisation.

title: The Mango Song

description: Pixies' environmental fever dream from Doolittle — sludge, ozone, biblical numerology and a string section. It was their first US major-label single and reached No. 5 on Billboard's Modern Rock chart.

pops.text: Black Francis had the hook — 'this monkey's gone to heaven' — long before he had the rest of the song. The whole track was built outwards from that one line.

Once he'd set it to music, Francis rushed to guitarist Joey Santiago's apartment early one morning to play it. Santiago remembers him laughing as he sang the 'If man is five' part: 'It was hilarious.'
The counting is Francis's loose take on Hebrew numerology: man is five, the devil is six, God is seven. He admitted to Alternative Press: 'I didn't go to the library and figure it out.'

The verses are environmental: an underwater god — Neptune — is 'killed by ten million pounds of sludge from New York to New Jersey,' while a creature in the sky gets stuck in the hole in the ozone layer.
Those strings exist because producer Gil Norton watched Kim Deal plucking the strings inside a grand piano during recording — and decided the song needed a string section.

The strings were cut in one session on 4 December 1988 at Carriage House Studios. There were no written scores: cellist Arthur Fiacco, who arrived in formal dress straight from an afternoon concert, wrote his part on the spot from riffs Francis showed him.

That made 'Monkey' the first Pixies song to feature guest musicians: two cellists and two violinists are credited, though Fiacco says he sent the other cellist home and played all the cello parts himself.
Released in March 1989, it was the first single from Doolittle and Pixies' first American major-label release, after signing to Elektra at the end of 1988.

It reached No. 5 on the US Modern Rock Tracks chart but only No. 60 in the UK. Critics disagreed with British buyers: Melody Maker named it Single of the Year, and Rolling Stone later placed it on its 500 Greatest Songs list.

The black-and-white clip — searchlights, slow motion, drifting fog and brief flashes of colour — was Pixies' first music video. The string players never appear. The Doolittle cover echoes the song instead: a haloed monkey beside the numbers five, six and seven.

title: Monkey Gone to Heaven
